c.entradas.etana.nombre_original: Etana (Akkadian); 'the shepherd who ascended to heaven' in the Sumerian King List
c.entradas.etana.fecha_texto: There are Old Babylonian, Middle Assyrian and Standard Babylonian versions (Neo-Assyrian copies from Nineveh). Scenes of a man riding on an eagle's back on Akkadian seals (c. 2300 BC) may depict the legend, although this is debated.
c.entradas.etana.resumen: Etana, king of Kish, has no children. An eagle that betrayed a serpent has been thrown into a pit as punishment; Etana rescues it, and it flies him up to heaven in search of the 'plant of birth'. The ending has been lost.
c.entradas.etana.interpretacion:
The story combines an animal fable about an oath broken before Shamash, the god of justice, with a problem of legitimacy: a king needs an heir for kingship to continue. The descriptions of the Earth seen from ever higher up are a much-cited literary device.

The Sumerian King List includes Etana among the post-flood kings of Kish and gives him a son, Balih. Many scholars conclude from this that the quest ultimately succeeded.
c.entradas.etana.detalles.0: The eagle and the serpent swear friendship before Shamash. The eagle breaks the oath by eating the serpent's young.
c.entradas.etana.detalles.1: Shamash helps the serpent take revenge by throwing the eagle into a pit.
c.entradas.etana.detalles.2: In the King List, Etana reigns for more than 1,500 years and is succeeded by his son Balih.
c.entradas.etana.detalles.3: Some Akkadian-period seals show a man riding on an eagle's back, which may be the oldest depiction of the myth.
c.entradas.nergal-ereshkigal.fecha_texto: A short version, of about 90 lines, on a tablet from Tell el-Amarna (14th century BC). A long Standard Babylonian version on Neo-Assyrian tablets from Sultantepe (8th–7th centuries BC) and a late copy from Uruk.
c.entradas.nergal-ereshkigal.resumen: The gods hold a banquet, and Ereshkigal, who cannot leave the Underworld, sends her vizier Namtar to collect her share. Nergal does not rise before him as a sign of respect and therefore has to go down to the Underworld. There he ends up uniting with Ereshkigal and becomes king of the world of the dead alongside her.
c.entradas.nergal-ereshkigal.interpretac:
The myth explains why Nergal, a god of war and plague linked to Kutha, became lord of the Underworld and husband of Ereshkigal. In this way it reconciles two traditions that were previously independent. The two versions differ: in the Amarna version, Nergal overpowers Ereshkigal by force and she offers to marry him; in the Sultantepe version there is a six-day romance, an escape and a return.

The text shows that the Mesopotamian Underworld has its own order and laws. It also shows the distance between the gods of heaven and those of the world below, who cannot visit each other freely.
c.entradas.nergal-ereshkigal.detalles.0: Namtar is Ereshkigal's vizier and appears in several Underworld texts.
c.entradas.nergal-ereshkigal.detalles.1: In the Amarna version, Nergal descends accompanied by fourteen demons.
c.entradas.nergal-ereshkigal.detalles.2: Ea advises Nergal not to accept food, drink, a seat or a bath in the Underworld.
c.entradas.nergal-ereshkigal.detalles.3: The Sultantepe version was published by O. R. Gurney (1960) and, in a modern edition, by Ponchia and Luukko (2013).
c.entradas.lugal-e.nombre_original: lugal-e ud me-lam2-bi nir-ĝal2 (Sumerian, 'King, storm of majestic splendor'); ETCSL 1.6.2
c.entradas.lugal-e.fecha_texto: Old Babylonian copies (c. 1900–1700 BC). It may have been composed in Ur III or earlier (debated). In the 1st millennium BC it was copied in bilingual Sumerian-Akkadian versions.
c.entradas.lugal-e.resumen: Ninurta, Enlil's warrior, fights in the mountains against Asag, a demon who fathered an army of stones with the Earth. After defeating him, Ninurta piles up stones to form the mountains (hursag) and channels the waters into the Tigris for irrigation. Then he judges each stone, giving it a useful function or a punishment.
c.entradas.lugal-e.interpretacion:
It is a myth that explains the origin of the mountains, of irrigation and of the properties of minerals. Ninurta, god of agriculture and of war, appears as guarantor of order against the chaotic forces that come from the mountains. The 'judgment of the stones' explains why some, such as diorite or carnelian, were used for statues and jewelry, while others were scorned.

At the end, Ninurta gives his mother Ninmah the name Ninhursag, 'lady of the mountain'. It was copied for more than a millennium and was one of the most studied Sumerian texts in the scribal schools.
c.entradas.lugal-e.detalles.0: It has about 720 lines, making it one of the longest Sumerian compositions.
c.entradas.lugal-e.detalles.1: Ninurta's talking weapon, Sharur, informs him about the enemy.
c.entradas.lugal-e.detalles.2: Asag is the son of An and Ki (the Earth).
c.entradas.lugal-e.detalles.3: Ninurta changes his mother's name from Ninmah to Ninhursag.
c.entradas.lugal-e.fuentes_primarias.1: Bilingual copies from Nineveh and Babylon (1st millennium BC)
c.entradas.inanna-enki-me.nombre: Inanna and Enki (the theft of the me)
c.entradas.inanna-enki-me.fecha_texto: Old Babylonian copies, c. 1900–1700 BC. It is known mainly from a large tablet from Nippur.
c.entradas.inanna-enki-me.resumen: Inanna visits Enki in his temple at Eridu. During a banquet, a drunken Enki gives her more than a hundred me, the powers and norms of civilization. Inanna carries them off to Uruk in the Boat of Heaven, and Enki, now sober, sends his vizier Isimud and several monsters to recover them, without success.
c.entradas.inanna-enki-me.interpretacion:
It is usually interpreted as a mythical explanation of how Uruk gained religious and cultural prestige at the expense of Eridu, the oldest city according to tradition. The text lists the me: kingship, priesthood, crafts, arts, sexual activity, war, judgment, the playing of instruments and many more. That list is one of the main sources for understanding the concept.

The me are not technological objects. They are principles of order that can be possessed, handed over and transported, a concrete way of thinking about abstract norms. The tone of the story has something comic about it.
c.entradas.inanna-enki-me.detalles.0: Enki hands over the me in fourteen batches, toasting with beer.
c.entradas.inanna-enki-me.detalles.1: Inanna travels in the Boat of Heaven, ma2-an-na.
c.entradas.inanna-enki-me.detalles.2: Enki sends Isimud, his two-faced vizier, with the enkum and lahama monsters to stop the boat at seven points.
c.entradas.inanna-enki-me.detalles.3: The list includes more than a hundred me, although several passages are broken.
c.entradas.an-anu.nombre_original: An (Sumerian, 'sky'); Anu(m) (Akkadian); written with the DINGIR sign, 'god, sky'
c.entradas.an-anu.fecha_texto: Attested from the 3rd millennium BC. His cult in Uruk was revived in the Seleucid period (3rd–2nd centuries BC).
c.entradas.an-anu.resumen: God of the sky and father of the gods. He stands at the top of the pantheon but plays little part in the myths. His main city is Uruk, where he shared the Eanna sanctuary with Inanna.
c.entradas.an-anu.interpretacion:
Jacobsen described him as the embodiment of authority: he is the source of kingship and power rather than an active god. In practice, Enlil wields executive power. In the scribes' numerical theology, An is assigned 60, the highest and most perfect number of the sexagesimal system.

In the 1st millennium BC, Anu regains prominence in Uruk, where Seleucid priests build him the great Bit Resh temple. The expression 'the gods called Anunnaki' probably means 'offspring of An' or 'princely offspring'.
c.entradas.an-anu.detalles.1: His consort is Ki (the Earth) in the Sumerian tradition and Antu in the Akkadian one.
c.entradas.an-anu.detalles.2: The cuneiform sign DINGIR, a star, serves at once for 'An', 'sky' and as a marker of divinity.
c.entradas.an-anu.detalles.3: In Uruk he had the 'White' ziggurat (Uruk period) and, much later, the Seleucid Bit Resh.
c.entradas.an-anu.fuentes_primarias.0: Texts from Uruk from the Uruk and Seleucid periods
c.entradas.enlil.fecha_texto: Attested from c. 2600 BC. He was the effective supreme god until, at the end of the 2nd millennium BC, Marduk took his place in Babylon.
c.entradas.enlil.resumen: Son of An and effective king of the gods. He grants kingship to human rulers and decrees destiny. His temple, the Ekur at Nippur, was the religious center of Sumer.
c.entradas.enlil.interpretacion:
Nippur was never a political capital, but Enlil's recognition in the Ekur legitimized the kings of any city that wanted to dominate Sumer. That is why the city carried so much ideological weight. In the myths, Enlil is an ambivalent figure: he guarantees order, but he also sends the flood and the plagues in Atrahasis.

The Enuma Elish transfers the 'Enlilship', that is, Enlil's title, to Marduk, and in Assyria Ashur was identified with him. His name has been translated as 'Lord Wind', but the etymology is unclear.
c.entradas.enlil.detalles.0: His main temple is the Ekur ('mountain house') at Nippur.
c.entradas.enlil.detalles.1: His consort is Ninlil and his main son is Ninurta. Nanna-Sin is also his son.
c.entradas.enlil.detalles.3: He is the original holder of the Tablet of Destinies in the myth of Anzu.
c.entradas.enki-ea.nombre_original: En-ki (Sumerian, 'Lord of the earth', etymology debated); Ea (Akkadian)
c.entradas.enki-ea.fecha_texto: Attested from the 3rd millennium BC and worshiped throughout Mesopotamian history.
c.entradas.enki-ea.resumen: God of wisdom, magic, the underground fresh waters (Apsu) and the crafts. His city is Eridu. In the myths he usually solves problems through cunning and protects humankind, as in the flood.
c.entradas.enki-ea.interpretacion:
Enki is the god 'who knows'. He is patron of the exorcists (āšipu), the craftsmen and the apkallu sages, and so he appears as a protector of culture. His ingenuity sometimes borders on deceit, as in Adapa or in Atrahasis, where he gets around his oath by speaking to a wall.

His iconographic symbol is the streams of water with fish flowing from his shoulders or from a vessel, and his animal is the goat-fish (suhurmāšu), forerunner of Capricorn. In late Babylonian theology he is the father of Marduk.
c.entradas.enki-ea.detalles.0: His main temple is the E-abzu or E-engura at Eridu.
c.entradas.enki-ea.detalles.2: In the iconography of Akkadian seals he appears with streams of water and fish coming from his shoulders.
c.entradas.enki-ea.detalles.3: His vizier is the two-faced Isimud (Usmû).
c.entradas.enki-ea.detalles.4: He is the father of Marduk in the Enuma Elish.
c.entradas.inanna-ishtar.fecha_texto: Her symbol, the knotted bundle of reeds, already appears in the Uruk period (c. 3300–3100 BC). Her cult lasts until the Seleucid period.
c.entradas.inanna-ishtar.resumen: Goddess of love, sexuality and war, identified with the planet Venus. She was the great goddess of Uruk. She is the most important female deity in Mesopotamia and the protagonist of numerous myths and hymns.
c.entradas.inanna-ishtar.interpretacion:
Inanna/Ishtar brings together opposing aspects: she is lover and warrior, young and powerful; she transgresses norms and at the same time embodies them. Many scholars attribute this complexity to syncretism between the Sumerian Inanna and the Semitic Ishtar, as well as local goddesses. Sargon of Akkad and his daughter Enheduanna, a priestess and the supposed author of hymns such as 'Nin-me-šara', promoted her as imperial patron.

As Venus, the morning and evening star, she is a key astral figure. The Venus observations of Ammi-saduqa are associated with her. The existence of a 'sacred marriage' rite between the goddess and the king is debated; the texts mention it, but its actual practice is a matter of debate.
c.entradas.inanna-ishtar.detalles.0: Her main temple is the Eanna at Uruk.
c.entradas.inanna-ishtar.detalles.1: Her symbols are the eight-pointed star, the knotted bundle of reeds and the lion.
c.entradas.inanna-ishtar.detalles.2: In Assyria she had major cult centers at Nineveh and Arbela.
c.entradas.inanna-ishtar.detalles.3: The Ishtar Gate of Babylon was built by Nebuchadnezzar II (c. 575 BC).
